t: You sit on a train. The train moves. Are you moving?
You are on a moving train, sitting still. Are you moving?
A passenger sits at rest on a moving train. Is the passenger in motion?
An object is at rest in a reference frame moving at constant velocity. Is the object in motion?
sub: It depends who is asking. Motion is not a yes-or-no question.
To someone outside, yes. To you, no. Both are right.
The answer depends on the reference frame. There is no privileged frame.
Galilean relativity: motion is frame-dependent. No inertial frame is preferred.

question: You throw a ball straight up on a moving train. Where does it land?
On a moving train, you throw a ball straight up. Where does it come down?
A ball is thrown vertically upward on a moving train. Where does it land relative to the thrower?
A projectile is launched vertically in a moving reference frame. Where does it land relative to the launcher?
options: Behind you, because the train moved while it was in the air
In front of you, because the ball kept the train's speed
note: Most people get this wrong. Guess before you think too hard.
Predict first. The answer surprises almost everyone.
Form a hypothesis. Consider what the ball's horizontal velocity is, relative to the train.
Predict. Apply Galilean invariance: the ball retains the train's horizontal velocity in the ground frame.

stages.label: Whose view?
captions: You, on the train. The ball goes up and comes straight down.
Your friend, on the platform. The ball goes up — but also forward, because the train is moving.
A bird, flying alongside. The ball goes up and forward, but slower than from the platform.
An astronaut, looking down. The train, the platform, and the bird are all moving — the ball traces a curve through all of them.
t: Move the slider to see the same ball throw from different viewpoints.
Drag the slider. Same throw, four viewpoints. The ball does the same thing — the description changes.
after: Same ball, same throw. The only thing that changed was who was watching. That is what frames of reference means.
Four observers, four descriptions, one motion. The frame of reference is the difference — not the physics.

stages.label: Whose view?
captions: Train frame: ball moves vertically. x = 0, y(t) = v₀t − ½gt².
Platform frame: ball has the train's horizontal velocity. x(t) = v_train·t, y(t) = v₀t − ½gt².
Bird frame (matching speed): ball moves vertically slower, as the bird cancels part of the train's motion.
Ground frame from above: ball traces a parabola in 2D. All frames agree on the physics; they disagree on the coordinates.
t: Work out what each observer sees before you reach the caption.
Predict each frame's description before the caption arrives. The invariance is in the physics, not the coordinates.
after: All four frames agree on the laws of motion. They disagree only on the numbers — and that disagreement is not a problem, it is the content of relativity.
Galilean invariance: the laws of mechanics are the same in all inertial frames. Coordinate differences are not physical differences.

t: Who is moving depends on who is watching. That is called a frame of reference.
The viewpoint you measure from is called a frame of reference. Motion is relative to it.
A frame of reference is the coordinate system you measure motion from. The same motion looks different from different frames.
A reference frame is a coordinate system with a specified state of motion. Galilean relativity: the laws of mechanics are invariant across inertial frames.
sub: There is no 'really moving'. Only moving relative to a frame.
No frame is more correct than another. Motion is always relative to a chosen frame.
Inertial frames (constant velocity) are equivalent under Galilean transformations.
No inertial frame is privileged. This is the principle of Galilean relativity, generalised by Einstein in 1905.

t: When you catch a ball, you are using frames of reference without knowing it.
Catching a ball is an intuitive frame-of-reference calculation. Your brain converts the ball's motion to your frame automatically.
A pilot docking a spacecraft must solve the relative-motion problem explicitly — the target's frame and the chaser's frame differ.
Rendezvous problems in orbital mechanics require explicit frame transformations. The ISS and a visiting capsule share inertial physics but differ in coordinate description.

q: You throw a ball straight up on a moving train. Where does it land?
A ball is thrown vertically on a moving train. Where does it land relative to the thrower?
On a train moving at constant velocity, a ball is thrown straight up. Where does it land?
In an inertial frame moving at constant velocity, a projectile is launched vertically. Where does it land relative to the launcher?
options: Back in your hand — the ball keeps the train's forward speed
Behind you — the train moved out from under it
In front of you — the ball accelerated forward
why: The ball was already moving forward with the train. Nothing pushes it backward, so it keeps that speed while it goes up and comes down — landing back in your hand.
The ball retains the train's horizontal velocity (inertia). In the train's frame, it goes straight up and down. In the platform's frame, it traces a parabola — but lands in your hand either way.
Galilean invariance: in the train's inertial frame, the ball's motion is purely vertical. Horizontal velocity is conserved, so it returns to the launch point in that frame.
The ball's velocity in the ground frame has a horizontal component equal to the train's. Gravity acts only vertically, so x(t) = v_train·t returns to x=0 in the train frame at t = 2v₀/g.

q: Is there a 'really moving' frame — one that is actually at rest?
Is any one frame the 'true' stationary frame?
Is there a privileged reference frame — one that is genuinely at rest?
Does a preferred rest frame exist?
options: No — motion is relative to whatever frame you choose
Yes, the ground is really at rest
Yes, the Sun is really at rest
why: There is no 'really moving'. The ground is moving with the Earth. The Earth moves around the Sun. The Sun moves through the galaxy. Every frame is relative to another.
No frame is the 'real' one. The ground is moving with Earth's rotation and orbit. The Sun moves through the galaxy. Motion is always relative to a chosen frame.
Galilean relativity: all inertial frames are equivalent. No experiment in mechanics can distinguish one inertial frame from another.

No preferred inertial frame exists. This is the principle of relativity, foundational to both Galilean and Einsteinian mechanics. (The cosmic microwave background does define a convenient frame, but not a privileged one.)
